description: ML Engineer excited to work with NASA data
summary:
PLaNETs is a trend-analysis tool built on top of 3 NASA dataset sources to answer natural-language questions about environmental trends with visualizations and reports of statistical significance. 

Users can ask about a trend in a variable or pair of variables over a specific time frame and location ("Has it gotten windier in Boston in the last five years?") and receive visualisations and analysis with statistical significance computed directly from the relevant variables using scikit-learn. Users are prompted to dig deeper with associated variables.

details:
PLaNETs: Plain-Language NASA Earth Trend Sleuth empowers students to ask questions about environmental trends in their own words!

It is a trend-analysis tool built on top of 3 NASA data sources to answer natural-language questions about environmental trends with visualizations and reports of statistical significance.

Ask a question in everyday words ("Is Boston getting more humid?"), compare two variables ("Have CO2 levels and ocean temps both been going up in Japan in the past decade?"), pick from dropdown menus, or browse variables.

The PLaNETS Sleuth uses scipy and matplotlib to produce a chart and a verdict on statistical significance. It offers a plain-language explanation using templates or an AI if an API key is given. It suggests 'clues' of other related trends the user can look at next, compares the data to nearby points, projects the years-to-significance of the trend if it is currently insignificant, and allows the user to train an LSTM to forecast the trend into the future.

1. The question is mapped to the variable and place of interest using a hybrid keyword + embedding search using BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 through fastembed.
2. The data for the variable of interest is fetched from the appropriate NASA dataset.

3. Seasonal cycles are removed from the data.

4. T-test and Mann-Kendall tests are completed and must agree to assess significance

5. Results are explained, either using a template or through an AI summary if an API key is provided

All statistics are computed in code. Generative AI is used only to parse questions as an alternative to the document embedding, and to word the explanation (if enabled). The app works fully end-to-end without an AI API Key.

PLaNETS turns NASA tools into answers in an approachable and educational way. It includes a glossary and tooltips on all statistics. It is intended for use by students, teachers, journalists, and interested citizen scientists. Ask questions directly to NASA datasets without sifting through them!

Datasets:

  • NASA POWER monthly point API: weather and climate variables from MERRA-2 and CERES, no login
  • NASA GES DISC Giovanni (“Giovanni in the Cloud” time series API): 867 satellite and model variables, using the visitor’s own Earthdata token
  • NASA PO.DAAC (via CMR and cloud OPeNDAP): sea surface temperature and sea level
  • NASA Worldview / GIBS imagery for the “See it from space” panel


Other data

  • GeoNames (CC BY 4.0): offline lookup for about 34,000 cities, every country and every US state

Statistics and analysis

  • NumPy, pandas: time series handling, removing the seasonal cycle
  • SciPy: OLS trend with t-test and 95% interval, Mann-Kendall test, Sen’s slope, correlation with autocorrelation-adjusted significance
  • matplotlib: all charts

Machine learning and search

  • LSTM written from scratch in NumPy: backpropagation, Adam optimizer, gradient-checked, with rolling-origin backtests
  • fastembed with BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 (ONNX Runtime, no PyTorch): meaning-based variable search
  • scikit-learn TF-IDF: keyword search, merged with the embeddings by reciprocal rank fusion
  • A hand-written phrase lexicon, and a retrieval eval set (main plus held-out questions)

AI (optional)

  • Anthropic Claude (Haiku 5.5) via the anthropic SDK: parses questions and words explanations from computed numbers only, with a daily call cap. The app works fully without it.

App and hosting

  • Streamlit (1.50+), deployed on Streamlit Community Cloud
  • requests for the NASA APIs, run in parallel with Python thread pools
  • netCDF4 for reading PO.DAAC data

Development tools

  • uv for dependencies and the lock file
  • Git and GitHub
  • Streamlit AppTest plus custom test scripts (unit tests, simulation checks, full-app smoke tests)
  • MLflow (optional local logging of each investigation)
  • Claude as a coding assistant

Hardware: Developed on a Windows laptop; runs on free-tier hosting without a GPU.

Factors I considered:

  • statistical honesty (two tests must agree, autocorrelation correction, lag scans are tagged as exploratory)
  • privacy (Earthdata and optional Claude tokens stay in the session)
  • cost (no endpoints or necessary metered APIs)
  • reliability (works with no AI key, caching, parallel fetches)
  • data credits

Creative elements:

The flow of the app is structured as a detective game: you ask, the app finds evidence, and suggests further clues for you to investigate, encouraging a chain of questions to flow naturally.

AI is used for words and code is used for numbers. Nothing can be invented. The document embedding used to search variables allows users to be loosey-goosey in their search queries ("Is california really getting muggier?" will prompt a humidity analysis over time).

Results are honest! Trends can be marked as 'not significant yet' and years-until significance is displayed. LSTMs are tested against held-out data, and when it adds nothing, that's reported too.

Shareable links allow students to share their findings with teachers, or cite claims generated in the app directly.

Technical Tradeoffs and Future Work: The embedding model and LSTM are implemented locally within the Streamlit app to limit the number of endpoints and moving pieces in the project. Streamlit's limited free-tier memory necessitates a small document embedding. In the future, I would use a larger embedding model such as bge-large, fine-tune it using SageMaker on a dataset with synthetic question/variable name pairs, and host it on a SageMaker endpoint. Instead of an LSTM, I would train a global Temporal Fusion Transformer and host it on SageMaker as well.
